Des Moines Lutheran Medical Center
NEPHROLOGY CONSULTATION
Patient: Brandvold, Curtis R    MRN: 71-440-2286    DOB: 09/27/1955    Room: 5W-512
Date of Consult: 05/19/2025    Consultant: Temperance Oyelade, MD    Referring Physician: Hugo Marchbanks, DO (Hospitalist)

Reason for Consultation: Worsening renal function and hyperkalemia.

History of Present Illness: 69-year-old man with type 2 diabetes complicated by diabetic nephropathy, hypertension, and chronic kidney disease stage 4 (baseline creatinine 2.8, eGFR 24 in January 2025) admitted 2 days ago with cellulitis of the left lower leg. Creatinine on admission 3.4, today 4.1, potassium 6.1. He received IV vancomycin for 48 hours with troughs up to 24. Urine output about 900 mL/24 h. Reports decreased appetite and mild nausea over the past month, no pruritus, no confusion. Not yet seen by transplant or dialysis access surgery.

Past Medical History: Type 2 DM x 22 years, diabetic retinopathy s/p laser, hypertension, peripheral arterial disease, gout.

Outpatient Medications: insulin glargine 28 units nightly, insulin lispro sliding scale, losartan 100 mg daily, amlodipine 10 mg daily, allopurinol 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg daily.

Allergies: No known drug allergies.

Physical Exam: BP 164/92, HR 84, afebrile. Alert and oriented. No asterixis. Lungs with faint bibasilar crackles. No pericardial rub. 2+ edema bilateral lower extremities, left leg erythema improving.

Data: Na 134, K 6.1, HCO3 17, BUN 78, Cr 4.1, phosphorus 6.2, calcium 8.3, albumin 3.0, Hgb 8.9, PTH 312. UA 3+ protein, no casts. Renal US: echogenic kidneys 9.2 and 9.6 cm, no hydronephrosis.

Impression:
1. Acute kidney injury on chronic kidney disease stage 4 (N17.9, N18.4), likely vancomycin related plus volume, superimposed on progressive diabetic nephropathy (E11.22).
2. Hyperkalemia (E87.5) and metabolic acidosis (E87.2).
3. Anemia in chronic kidney disease (D63.1).
4. Secondary hyperparathyroidism of renal origin (N25.81).

Recommendations:
- Stop vancomycin, switch to cefazolin renally dosed per pharmacy.
- Hold losartan. Sodium zirconium cyclosilicate 10 g TID x 48 h, low potassium diet.
- Sodium bicarbonate 650 mg TID.
- Strict I/O, daily BMP. No indication for urgent dialysis today.
- Begin CKD education; vein preservation left arm, no IVs or blood draws.
- Iron studies; consider ESA as outpatient.
- Outpatient nephrology follow up within 2 weeks of discharge.

Thank you for this consultation. Will follow.
Temperance Oyelade, MD - Nephrology

OPERATIVE REPORT
Patient: Arredondo, Felipe S.   MRN: FMS-2210457   DOB: 07/07/1972
Date of Surgery: 09/14/2023
Surgeon: Constance Mbeki-Harlan, MD
Assistant: Rhett Galloway, PA-C
Anesthesia: General endotracheal - Viktor Salinas, MD

Preoperative Diagnosis: Symptomatic cholelithiasis with chronic cholecystitis.
Postoperative Diagnosis: Chronic cholecystitis with cholelithiasis (K80.10).
Procedure Performed: Laparoscopic cholecystectomy with intraoperative cholangiogram.

Indications: 51-year-old man with type 2 diabetes and obesity (BMI 38) with recurrent biliary colic over 6 months and ultrasound showing multiple gallstones and a thickened gallbladder wall. Risks, benefits and alternatives were discussed and informed consent was obtained.

Description of Procedure: The patient was brought to the operating room and placed supine. After induction of general anesthesia, the abdomen was prepped and draped in sterile fashion. A time-out was performed. A 12 mm Hasson port was placed at the umbilicus using open technique and pneumoperitoneum established to 15 mmHg. Three 5 mm ports were placed under direct vision in the epigastrium and right upper quadrant. The gallbladder was distended with omental adhesions to the fundus, which were taken down with blunt dissection. The fundus was retracted cephalad and the infundibulum laterally. The hepatocystic triangle was dissected and the critical view of safety obtained, with two structures entering the gallbladder and the lower third of the gallbladder separated from the liver bed. A cholangiogram through the cystic duct showed normal filling of the common bile duct and free flow into the duodenum without filling defects. The cystic duct and cystic artery were clipped twice proximally and once distally and divided. The gallbladder was removed from the liver bed with electrocautery and placed in a retrieval bag. Hemostasis of the liver bed was confirmed. The gallbladder was extracted through the umbilical site. The fascia was closed with 0 Vicryl and skin with 4-0 Monocryl.

Findings: Chronically inflamed gallbladder with multiple stones, normal cholangiogram.
Estimated Blood Loss: 15 mL
Specimens: Gallbladder with stones - please send to pathology for routine examination.
Drains: None
Complications: None
Condition: Stable to PACU, extubated.

Postoperative Plan: Discharge home today if tolerating diet. Resume metformin tomorrow. Follow up in clinic in 2 weeks.

Constance Mbeki-Harlan, MD

Hoosier Heartland Vascular Surgery - St. Wendelin Hospital
Operative Note

Patient: Brubaker, Harlan D.    DOB: 04/15/1951    MRN: 00331980    Date of Service: 07/08/2025
Surgeon: Gwendolyn Vandermeer-Lane, MD, FACS
First Assistant: Devin Nwachukwu, MD (resident)
Anesthesia: General

Preoperative diagnosis: Symptomatic stenosis of the left internal carotid artery, 85%, with transient ischemic attack 06/2025.
Postoperative diagnosis: Same. Occlusion and stenosis of left carotid artery (I65.22).

Operation: Left carotid endarterectomy with bovine pericardial patch angioplasty.

Indications: 74-year-old man with two episodes of transient right hand weakness and expressive aphasia. Carotid duplex and CTA confirmed 85% left ICA stenosis. Comorbidities include coronary artery disease, type 2 diabetes with peripheral angiopathy, hypertension, and prior tobacco use.

Description: After induction, the patient was positioned with neck extended and rotated right. EEG monitoring was established. An incision was made along the anterior border of the sternocleidomastoid. The common, internal and external carotid arteries were exposed and controlled; the hypoglossal nerve was identified and protected. After systemic heparin 5000 units, the arteries were clamped. EEG showed no changes, so no shunt was required. Arteriotomy was carried from the common carotid into the internal carotid beyond the plaque. A heavily calcified, ulcerated plaque was removed with a clean distal endpoint. The arteriotomy was closed with a bovine pericardial patch using 6-0 Prolene. Flow was restored to the external then internal carotid. Doppler signals were strong and triphasic. Protamine was given. The wound was closed in layers.

Clamp time: 32 minutes. EBL: 100 mL. Complications: none.
Patient awakened neurologically intact and moved to PACU.

Plan: Continue aspirin and clopidogrel, atorvastatin 80 mg. Neuro checks q1h. BP goal systolic 100-150.

G. Vandermeer-Lane, MD
